Shanlin Zhou     Xinpeng Wang     Jianxun Lian     Zhenghao Liu  Affiliation: Laks V.S. Lakshmanan , Xiaoyuan Yi* , and Yongtao Hao* 
Abstract

Trained on diverse human-authored texts, Large Language Models (LLMs) unlocked the potential for Creative Natural Language Generation (CNLG), benefiting various applications like advertising and storytelling. Nevertheless, CNLG still remains difficult due to two main challenges. (1) Multi-objective flexibility: user requirements are often personalized, fine-grained, and pluralistic, which LLMs struggle to satisfy simultaneously; (2) Interpretive complexity: beyond generation, creativity also involves understanding and interpreting implicit meaning to enhance users’ perception. These challenges significantly limit current methods, especially in short-form text generation, in generating creative and insightful content. To address this, we focus on Chinese baby naming, a representative short-form CNLG task requiring adherence to explicit user constraints (e.g., length, semantics, anthroponymy) while offering meaningful aesthetic explanations. We propose NAMeGEn, a novel multi-agent optimization framework that iteratively alternates between objective extraction, name generation, and evaluation to meet diverse requirements and generate accurate explanations. To support this task, we further construct a classical Chinese poetry corpus with 17k+ poems to enhance aesthetics, and introduce CBNames, a new benchmark with tailored metrics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NAMeGEn effectively generates creative names that meet diverse, personalized requirements while providing meaningful explanations, outperforming six baseline methods spanning various LLM backbones without any training.

Index Terms: 
Creative NLG, Multi-Objective Optimization, Collaborative Multi-Agents Framework.

I Introduction

Benefiting from large-scale model parameters and extensive training data, large language models (LLMs) [1, 2, 3, 4] have not only achieved notable breakthroughs in language understanding [5, 6] and reasoning [7, 8, 9], but also unlocked the potential of Creative Natural Language Generation (CNLG) [10, 11, 12]. As a special case of controllable language generation [13, 14], CNLG emphasizes the novelty, distinctiveness, and aesthetics of generated text, which empowers a spectrum of downstream tasks [15, 16, 17], spanning from poetry generation [18, 19, 20], story writing [21, 22], summarization [23, 24, 25], and slogan generation [26].

Existing CNLG studies [10, 18, 27, 28, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 26, 29, 30] mainly focus on achieving general objectives, e.g., creativity, fluency, and coherence. However, in real-world CNLG applications, e.g., naming design and slogan creation, existing methods face two primary challenges. Challenge 1: Multi-objective flexibility. User requirements for creativity are often personalized, fine-grained, and multi-objective [31, 32, 33], while LLMs struggle to satisfy these diverse goals simultaneously [34]. Challenge 2: Interpretive complexity. According to cognitive psychology theories [35, 36], creativity is not only reflected in the generation process, but also involves understanding and interpreting the implicit meanings [37] behind the content to enhance user perception. As illustrated in Fig. 1, in Naming Chinese Baby (NCB), a typical CNLG task, a generated name is required to meet multiple explicit user-specified requirements, e.g., traditional Chinese cultural significance, parents’ expectations for the baby, Bazi&Wuxing 11 1 Bazi&Wuxing are traditional cultural factors commonly used in Chinese baby naming. Bazi analyzes the birth date and time, while Wuxing represents the five elements (wood, fire, earth, metal, and water). Together, they provide insight into fate and fortune based on traditional Chinese numerology. and personal characteristics (see Fig. 2 for examples). Besides, corresponding high-quality explanations are needed to help users understand the underlying connection between the generated name and user requirements (like expectation), as well as implicit meanings and aesthetics. Such challenges place greater demands on the LLMs’ capabilities for understanding, integration, and interpretability. As a result, existing LLMs are often regarded as lacking human-level creativity [38, 39, 40].

These challenges are more pronounced in short-form CNLG [41, 42, 43] compared to the long-form one [44, 45], as LLMs need to integrate multiple, personalized, and fine-grained user requirements into a compact piece of text. Therefore, we focus on short-form CNLG, and propose two types of objectives grounded in the two challenges introduced above. (a) Explicit User-specified Objectives (EUOs) refer to creative requirements explicitly set by users, such as parents’ expectations in the NCB task. (b) Implicit Interpretive Objectives (IIOs) represent fundamental attributes, e.g., accuracy, completeness, and clarity, of LLMs’ explanation to connect the underlying meanings and aesthetics with generated text, which LLMs should satisfy by default. To sum up, short-form CNLG involves three goals: (i) EUOs optimization, (ii) IIOs improvement, and (iii) the balance of both.

These goals are highly relevant to addressing the attribute degradation issue in Multi-aspect Controllable Text Generation (MCTG) [46, 47, 48], where attribute imbalance or conflict arises during generation [49, 50, 51]. To handle this problem, early studies treated the decoding process as a Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) process [52] and applied various optimization strategies to balance the different attributes to some extent. Typical methods include MUCOCO [31], GDC [46], Mix&Match [53], COLD decoding [54] and MacLaSa [49]. Besides, prefix-tuning [55] was also adopted to achieve multi-attribute control [47, 48, 50, 51]. Nevertheless, these methods are mainly designed to satisfy a pre-defined set of attributes, e.g., toxicity, topic and sentiment, and thus fail to handle the flexible and fine-grained EUOs and IIOs (challenges 1 & 2). More recently, with the rapid development of LLMs, multi-aspect control of LLMs receives increasing attention, with a focus on multi-instruction constraint optimization via fine-tuning [56, 57, 58]. Despite good effectiveness, these methods require substantial computational or data costs. Moreover, fine-tuning requires access to model parameters, making these methods incompatible with closed-source LLMs.

In this work, we aim to tackle the multi-objective flexibility and interpretive complexity challenges of CNLG, and take NCB as a typical short-term CNLG task. Given the strong capabilities of LLMs in generation [59] and real-world applications [60, 61, 62], we resort to In-Context Learning (ICL) [63] and multi-agent framework [60] to avoid unaffordable costs and achieve better flexibility and creativity. Since existing related work predominantly concentrates on reasoning tasks and thus is less suitable for multi-objective optimization issues [64, 65, 66], we propose a Novel Agent-based Multi-Personalized-Goal Enhancement Framework (NAMeGEn) to tackle the two challenges and achieve EUOs and IIOs. As shown in Fig. 2, NAMeGEn performs a two-stage process, i.e., multi-objective information preparation and dynamic iterative objective optimization, which are executed through three agents, namely, Multi-Objective Manager (MOM), Multi-Objective Generator (MOG), and Multi-Objective Evaluator (MOE). MOM is responsible for task analysis and information processing, while MOG generates a creative result by integrating user queries with MOM-processed information. MOE participates in evaluating MOM’s search to support MOG’s generation and assesses MOG’s outputs to ensure a balanced multi-objective creative outcome. The three agents collectively work on key information extraction, dynamic generation, and objective evaluation in an alternating and interactive manner, towards ultimately achieving optimal creative outcomes. The whole framework is backbone-agnostic, training-free, and efficient, allowing the integration with arbitrary either open-source or black-box LLMs. Since we select NCB as a typical CNLG task to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we further develop a benchmark named CBNames. Given that cultural meaning (e.g., aesthetics and poeticness) is often considered in Chinese names and LLMs might produce hallucinations, we further collect an ancient Chinese poetry dataset (denoted as CPoetry), utilize it via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [67], and design novel tailored metrics for this task considering both EUOs and IIOs. Experiments on various LLM backbones demonstrate the efficacy and superiority of NAMeGEn in short-term multi-objective CNLG, outperforming six recent strong baselines.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose NAMeGEn, a novel framework for solving hybrid multi-objective optimization in short-term CNLG tasks. With training-free dynamic iterative optimization strategies, NAMeGEn achieves a balance among multi-EUOs, multi-IIOs, and the trade-offs between them, improving content quality and ensuring applicability across both open-source and closed-source models.

  • •

    We have developed a benchmark (CBNames) for the NCB task and created a new classical poetry retrieval database (CPoetry) to reduce hallucinations in LLMs.

  • •

    Our framework outperforms existing methods across all six backbone models, demonstrating superior creative generation and enhanced interpretability without requiring model-specific training.

II Related Work

Creative Natural Language Generation (CNLG) is a long-standing research area, with classic tasks including poetry generation [19, 20], story writing [21, 22], summarization [23, 24], and slogan generation [26]. These studies primarily focus on objectives such as novelty, originality, fluency, and diversity of generated text. While these metrics are vital for assessing generation quality, they often overlook more personalized and nuanced goals required in real-world applications. In practice, existing approaches struggle with multi-objective flexibility (challenge 1). On the other hand, most prior work emphasizes generation outcomes while underestimating the importance of interpretation for user understanding. Creativity also involves understanding and explaining implicit meanings, as highlighted by cognitive psychology theories [35, 36]. However, current methods largely ignore interpretive complexity (challenge 2). Our work addresses these challenges by introducing task analysis and dynamic multi-objective evaluation strategies.

Multi-Aspect Controllable Text Generation (MCTG) aims to generate text that satisfies multiple attribute constraints (e.g., sentiment, topic, style). While traditional methods often focus on single-aspect control, extending to multi-aspect scenarios introduces challenges like attribute interference and degeneration [46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 51]. Some works frame MCTG as a multi-objective optimization (MOO) problem. MUCOCO [31] first formalizes MCTG as MOO by jointly optimizing through gradient descent for multiple attributes in the loss function. Similarly, [68] treats detoxification as a multi-objective problem involving non-toxicity, semantic preservation, and fluency. However, these works mainly target general attributes like toxicity, formality, or style, while overlooking more practical objectives, such as flexible, fine-grained user instructions and implicit interpretive goals. Although recent work [57, 56, 58, 69, 10] explores multi-constraint instruction following, few adopt explicit MOO frameworks, making it difficult to manage conflicting constraints effectively.

LLM Based Multi-Agent. Given the strong reasoning and planning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), LLM-based agents have seen rapid development. Compared to single-agent systems that solve problems through tool use and interactions with external environments, multi-agent systems emphasize decision-making through role-playing and communication among multiple agents [70, 71, 72]. However, the use of multi-agent systems has primarily focused on solving complex tasks [30, 73, 74]. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has explored leveraging multi-agent collaboration to explicitly address multi-objective tasks, which is a gap our work seeks to fill.

III Methodlogy

III-A Overview

In this section, we formally introduce the task of multi-objective optimization in creative natural language generation (CNLG) and the proposed method. CNLG involves optimizing explicit user-specified objectives (EUOs), implicit interpretive objectives (IIOs), and the trade-offs between them, constituting a hybrid multi-objective optimization problem. The goal of CNLG is to achieve optimization over this hybrid multi-objective setting. First, we formalize this task as follows:

Y=arg⁡maxθ⁡f⁡(x,Oexp,Oimp)Y=\arg\max_{\theta}f(x,O_{\text{exp}},O_{\text{imp}}) (1)

where Y={r,E}Y=\{r,E\} denotes the final output of it, with the generated text rr and a set of explanations EE. For example, in the Naming Chinese Baby (NCB) task, rr is the generated name, and EE is the corresponding set of explanations detailing how the name reflects each objective. θ\theta is a dynamic optimization parameter, xx is input, Oexp={o1e,o2e,…,ome}O_{\text{exp}}=\{o^{e}_{1},o^{e}_{2},\dots,o^{e}_{m}\} and Oimp={o1i,o2i,…,oni}O_{\text{imp}}=\{o^{i}_{1},o^{i}_{2},\dots,o^{i}_{n}\} means mm EUOs, IIOs respectively, EE is also composed of mm individual explanations {e1,e2,…,em}\{e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{m}\}, corresponding to EUOs.

In our work, we design a training-free and multi-agent collaborative architecture, NAMeGEn, to reach this aim. The overview of NAMeGEn is shown in Fig. 2. Our pipeline is collaboratively executed by three intelligent agents, including the Multi-Objective Manager (MOM) AMA_{\text{M}}, the Multi-Objective Generator (MOG) AGA_{\text{G}}, and the Multi-Objective Evaluator (MOE) AEA_{\text{E}} (as shown in the green block of Fig. 2). Next, we divide the whole pipeline into two stages. The first stage is multi-objective information preparation (see steps 1.1 and 1.2 in Fig. 2). It covers task analysis, key information extraction and expansion, EUO description, and interpretability requirement design, aiming to build a solid foundation for hybrid multi-objective generation. This stage is completed by collaboration between MOM AMA_{\text{M}} and MOE AEA_{\text{E}}. The second stage is dynamic iterative objective optimization (see steps 2 and 3 in Fig. 2). In this stage, MOG AGA_{\text{G}} drafts a creative output using information from MOM AMA_{\text{M}}, then dynamically and iteratively refines it based on MOE AEA_{\text{E}}’s evaluation and feedback against EUOs and IIOs. This way of optimization helps to progressively refine the CNLG by balancing hybrid multi-objectives. Next, we elaborate on each stage in detail.

III-B Multi-objective Information Preparation

This stage involves analyzing the creative task and processing multi-objective information, which aims to gain a deeper understanding of user personalized requirements and enhance the ability to interpret implicit meaning, helping to produce higher-quality creative results later.

III-B1 Task analysis process (see 1.1 in Fig. 2)

This includes identifying the task type Itype←AM​(x)I_{\text{type}}\leftarrow A_{\text{M}}(x) (e.g., naming a Chinese baby), get Oexp={o1e,o2e,…,ome}O_{\text{exp}}=\{o^{e}_{1},o^{e}_{2},\dots,o^{e}_{m}\}, and estimating user preference scores for OexpO_{\text{exp}}. Specially, when EUOs OexpO_{\text{exp}} are not provided by user, MOM AMA_{\text{M}} can automatically parse appropriate EUOs, by 𝒪exp←AM​(Itype)\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}}\leftarrow A_{\text{M}}(I_{\text{type}}). However, when auto-parsing objectives, the model often parses similar ones (e.g., ”Harmonious Pronunciation”, ”Easy to Pronounce and Remember”, etc.). Therefore, we introduce evaluation, ensuring the independence and appropriateness of each objective. Then the final EUOs we get by 𝒪exp←AM​(Itype,b)\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}}\leftarrow A_{\text{M}}(I_{\text{type}},b), where the evaluation feedback b←AE​(𝒪exp,Itype)b\leftarrow A_{E}(\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}},I_{\text{type}}). We estimate user preference by Ipref←AM​(𝒪exp,x)I_{\text{pref}}\leftarrow A_{\text{M}}(\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}},x) and normalize it into a weight vector WexpW_{\text{exp}}. This helps to better meet different users’ personalized needs. Later, this weight WexpW_{\text{exp}} will work in the dynamic iterative objective optimization stage.

III-B2 Process multi-objective information (1.2 in Fig. 2)

This covers extracting and expanding information, retrieving related knowledge, and refining the EUOs’ description and explanatory requirements. Firstly, AMA_{\text{M}} extracts key content IkiI_{\text{ki}} (e.g., surname and date of birth in the naming task) from user input xx, for use in retrieval and expansion. If insufficient, it can infer additional details (e.g., deducing the birth season based on the date of birth) to enrich IkiI_{\text{ki}}. Next, we add a retrieval step (shown as in Algorithm 1) into AMA_{\text{M}} to mitigate the hallucination of LLMs in domain knowledge. User input xx, with its multi-aspect content, also makes this retrieval process a multi-objective task. Specifically, MOM AMA_{\text{M}} first uses information IkiI_{\text{ki}} to retrieve preliminary candidates R′R^{\prime}. Then, based on xx, it reconstructs a style-aligned query qq with the knowledge base (KB), to retrieve the top-kk candidates ℛ={r1,r2,…,rm}\mathcal{R}=\{r_{1},r_{2},\ldots,r_{m}\} from R′R^{\prime}, using an embedding-based retrieval strategy 22 2 https://huggingface.co/lier007/xiaobu-embedding-v2. Style rewriting for query qq can help to increase the efficiency of retrieval. To find the best knowledge IrkI_{\text{rk}}, we make MOE AEA_{\text{E}} participate in evaluation and rerank (see line 7 in Algorithm 1). During evaluation, if none is satisfactory, MOE AEA_{\text{E}} further revises the query qq but keeps its style. The revised query qq is fed back to MOM AMA_{\text{M}}, which discards previous results and performs a new retrieval from the remaining knowledge. This process iterates until the optimal IrkI_{\text{rk}} is found. To help MOG better understand EUOs and try to align with IIOs, MOM AMA_{\text{M}} designs separately detailed descriptions Idesc={c1,c2,…,cm}I_{\text{desc}}=\{c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{m}\} and explanatory requirements Ireqs={q1,q2,…,qm}I_{\text{reqs}}=\{q_{1},q_{2},\ldots,q_{m}\}. Descriptions IdescI_{\text{desc}} are more reliable information than EUOs’ keywords 𝒪exp\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}}, and requirements IreqsI_{\text{reqs}} help MOG AGA_{\text{G}} generate more accurate, complete, and clear content. Notably, their incorporation can effectively enhance the efficiency of the hybrid multi-objective optimization process, thereby contributing to the generation of creative outputs with improved quality and interpretability. MOE AEA_{\text{E}} is also involved in this process, ensuring the rationality of these contents by evaluation, feedback, and iteration. These steps are as follows:

(Idesc,Ireqs)←AM​(x,𝒪exp,Iki,Irk,b)(I_{\text{desc}},I_{\text{reqs}})\leftarrow A_{\text{M}}(x,\mathcal{O}_{\text{exp}},I_{\text{ki}},I_{\text{rk}},b) (2)
bd​e​t​a​i​l←AE​(Idesc,Ireqs)b_{detail}\leftarrow A_{E}(I_{\text{desc}},I_{\text{reqs}}) (3)

where bd​e​t​a​i​lb_{detail} is the evaluation feedback. Moreover, they will serve as crucial evaluation criteria in the dynamic iterative objective optimization stage. Ultimately, we obtain the expanded hybrid information set: ℐ={Itype,Ipref,Irk,Idesc,Ireqs}\mathcal{I}=\{I_{\text{type}},I_{\text{pref}},I_{\text{rk}},I_{\text{desc}},I_{\text{reqs}}\} All the above information is stored in MOM’s memory to facilitate interactions with other intelligent agents.

III-C Dynamic Iterative Objective Optimization

Algorithm 2 shows the process of this stage. MOG AMA_{\text{M}} utilizes the user query xx and the hybrid information ℐ\mathcal{I} from MOM to generate the initial results 𝒴={r,E}\mathcal{Y}=\{r,E\}, where rr is result and EE is its explanation set {e1j,e2j,…,emj}\{e^{j}_{1},e^{j}_{2},\ldots,e^{j}_{m}\}. Afterward, MOE AEA_{\text{E}} evaluates the completion of 𝒴\mathcal{Y} in EUOs and IIOs separately, based on IdescI_{\text{desc}} and IreqsI_{\text{reqs}}. Our work defines three IIOs—accuracy, completeness, and clarity—and evaluates this aspect first, as MOE AEA_{\text{E}}’s understanding of EUOs’ completion depends on them. Evaluating accuracy is essential for mitigating model hallucinations. In our work, MOE AEA_{\text{E}} adopts a rule-based approach FaccF_{\text{acc}} and refers to information II for evaluation. Given the subjectivity of completeness and clarity, rule-based methods are no longer applicable. Therefore, MOE AEA_{\text{E}} designs a new scoring mechanism to measure their performance respectively. To integrate them, we provide a trans-function:

θimp=Wimp⋅Simp\theta_{\text{imp}}=W_{\text{imp}}\cdot S_{\text{imp}} (4)
Wimp=[1n,1n,…,1n]∈ℝnW_{\text{imp}}=[\frac{1}{n},\frac{1}{n},\dots,\frac{1}{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n} (5)

where θimp\theta_{\text{imp}} represents the implicit performance, WimpW_{\text{imp}} is the weight vector, SimpS_{\text{imp}} is the score vector of IIOs. In this way, it mathematically converts the optimization for IIOs into a single-objective optimization problem.

We similarly evaluate each EUO and combine them to form the score vector SexpS_{\text{exp}}. Different from traditional optimization logic, due to the user input xx usually implying their potential preference for EUOs, it is necessary to decompose xx and obtain the preference IprefI_{\text{pref}} (from MOE AEA_{\text{E}}) as the optimization weight vector WexpW_{\text{exp}}. Here, EUOs’ unified quantitative result is:

θexp=Wexp⋅Sexp\theta_{\text{exp}}=W_{\text{exp}}\cdot S_{\text{exp}} (6)

Moreover, expected criteria ψimp\psi_{\text{imp}} and ψexp\psi_{\text{exp}} are introduced to judge implicit and explicit quantification results, respectively. It is worth noting that except for the generated content, the criteria ψimp\psi_{\text{imp}} and ψexp\psi_{\text{exp}} adjust dynamically with the iteration:

ψimp={δjimp<twδα⋅log⁡(jimp+tw)jimp>tw\psi_{\text{imp}}=\begin{cases}\delta&j_{\text{imp}}<t_{w}\\ \frac{\delta}{\alpha\cdot\log(j_{\text{imp}}+t_{\text{w}})}&j_{\text{imp}}>t_{\text{w}}\end{cases} (7)
ψexp={δjexp<twδα⋅log⁡(jexp+tw)jexp>tw\psi_{\text{exp}}=\begin{cases}\delta&j_{\text{exp}}<t_{w}\\ \frac{\delta}{\alpha\cdot\log(j_{\text{exp}}+t_{\text{w}})}&j_{\text{exp}}>t_{\text{w}}\end{cases} (8)

where jimpj_{\text{imp}} is implicit evaluation round counter, jexpj_{\text{exp}} is explicit evaluation round counter, twt_{\text{w}} is warmup round, δ\delta is initial threshold, and α\alpha is decay factor. Thanks to this dynamic iteration process, the generation quality is improved while multiple explicit objectives are achieved in balance.

IV Experiments

IV-A Experimental Setup

IV-A1 Datasets

To validate the effectiveness of our framework, we conduct Naming Chinese Babies (NCB) as a typical short-term Creative Natural Language Generation (CNLG) task. NCB is required to consider various factors in creating a short name, making it a significant challenge. Firstly, we use a large language model (LLM), through manual verification, to simulate 500 human naming requests, create a benchmark (called CNames). This data encompasses over 200 Chinese surnames, including compound surnames, and reflects a range of potential user considerations in the naming process, such as traditional Chinese cultural significance, parental expectations, the Bazi&Wuxing, personal characteristics, and other special requirements. User preferences are annotated per objective for each query. In China, parents often draw on classical poetry to give their names cultural depth. However, LLMs frequently make factual errors in the poetry domain. To address this, we collect and expand a dataset of classical Chinese poetry (called CPoetry) containing 176,450 entries with metadata such as poets, dynasties, titles, content, interpretations, and themes.

IV-A2 Baseline Methods

We compare our proposed framework, NAMeGEn, with the following methods. Base is the raw query with task description. CoT [75] involves appending the phrase “Let’s think step by step” to the input. TDB [76] is the zero-shot prompting with “Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step”. Few-shot [77] adds a few demonstration exemplars of question-answer in prompt. Q2Kw [78] integrates retrieved knowledge into the prompt by first using an LLM to generate results from the user’s raw requirement, then combining these results with the original requirement to form an extended query for knowledge retrieval. LLM-D [30] uses multiple agents to conduct a multi-stage discussion to complete a creative and diverse response task.

IV-A3 Evaluation and Metrics

Recent research has shown the capability of LLM to emulate human judgment and effectively evaluate content [79, 80, 81]. In this work, to evaluate quantitatively, we use both LLM and human evaluations.

In LLM evaluation, we propose metrics to evaluate the performance of Explicit User-specified Objectives (EUOs), Implicit Interpretive Objectives (IIOs), and their overall optimization. In other words, these are designed to evaluate how well different methods address Hybrid Multi-Objective Optimization (HMOO) and creative diversity in short-term CNLG. Firstly, for EUOs, we design Explicit multi-objective Completeness (EC) and Standard Deviation based EC (EC_std):

EC=1N​∑i=1N∑j=1mwi,j​si,j∑j=1mwi,j\text{EC}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_{i,j}s_{i,j}}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_{i,j}} (9)
EC_std=1N​∑i=1N1mi​∑j=1mi(si,j−1mi​∑j=1misi,j)2\text{EC\_std}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sqrt{\frac{1}{m_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{m_{i}}\left(s_{i,j}-\frac{1}{m_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{m_{i}}s_{i,j}\right)^{2}} (10)

where si,js_{i,j} and wi,jw_{i,j} denote the score and user weight for the the jj-th objective of ii-th sample, with mm EUOs and NN samples. si,js_{i,j} is scored by LLM. Higher EC implies better performance in achieving multi-EUOs. EC_std quantifies the balance of multi-EUOs’ performance via standard deviation, where a lower score means better. Secondly, we evaluate different IIOs’ performance, using ACC, CRC, LR, which separately measure hallucination degree, semantic quality (comprehensiveness, relevance, clarity), and logical consistency. For all of them, a higher score indicates better performance. Subsequently, we compute Implicit Multi-Objective Completeness (IC) and Standard Deviation based IC (IC_std). IC is the average of ACC, CRC, and LR. IC_std is their standard deviation. Higher IC indicates better multi-IIO performance, while lower IC_std reflects more balanced and stable results. The following describes the method for calculating IC_std:

IC_std=1N​∑i=1N13​∑k∈{A​C​C,C​R​C,L​R}(si,k−s¯i)2\text{IC\_std}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k\in\{ACC,CRC,LR\}}\left(s_{i,k}-\bar{s}_{i}\right)^{2}} (11)

where s¯i\bar{s}_{i} is the mean of the ii-th sample’s scores on ACC, CRC, and LR, with si,ks_{i,k} denoting the score for the kk-th objective. Finally, from a holistic view, we provide Comprehensive Multi-Objective Completeness (CC), Standard Deviation-based CC (CC_std), and Diversity (DIV). CC averages EC and IC; CC_std averages their standard deviations. DIV scores uniqueness across methods for the result of each sample, where if it appears in other methods, it scores 0; otherwise, 1. Higher DIV indicates better diversity. CC_std is calculated as follows:

CC_std=1N​∑i=1Nσi\text{CC\_std}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{i} (12)
σi=12​((ECi−x¯i)2+(ICi−x¯i)2)\sigma_{i}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left((\text{EC}_{i}-\bar{x}_{i})^{2}+(\text{IC}_{i}-\bar{x}_{i})^{2}\right)} (13)

where σi\sigma_{i} means the standard deviation, x¯i\bar{x}_{i} denote the average of EC and IC for sample ii. In short, EC and EC_std reflect the performance and balance of multi-EUO optimization. ACC, CRC, and LR measure explanation quality, while IC and IC_std evaluate the performance and balance of multi-IIO optimization. CC and CC_std can capture the overall completeness and balance of both EUOs and IIOs. DIV compares the diversity of results across methods.

In human evaluation, we randomly sample 50 test cases, each evaluated by 3 annotators on a 0–3 scale. EUOs are scored based on completeness, while IIOs are evaluated in CRC and LR. In addition, annotators are also asked to identify the best response among the different methods for each case.

IV-A4 Implementation Details

To ensure consistency, the NCB task prompt includes five objectives: traditional Chinese cultural significance, parental expectations, Bazi&Wuxing, personal characteristics, and other special requirements. We use the following seven LLMs as backbones: Qwen (long) [82], GLM-4 [83], DeepSeek (V3) [84], Mistral (small-latest) [85], emini (1.5-flash) [83], and GPT4o [59]. Among them, Qwen [82], GLM-4 [83] and DeepSeek [84] are LLMs proficient in Chinese, while Mistral [85], Gemini [83], and GPT-4o [59]are LLMs proficient in English. For DeepSeek [84], we adopt the recommended setting (temperature=1.5) to enhance creative generation. We use Kimi [86] as the LLM evaluator. ACC is computed via LLM extraction and rule-based methods. Other metrics, rated from 0 (invalid) to 3 (excellent), are averaged and normalized to a 0–100 scale.

IV-B Method Comparison

To demonstrate NAMeGEn’s effectiveness, we compare it with five baseline categories: Base, reasoning-based (CoT [75], TDB [76]), in-context (Few-shot [77]), retrieval-based (Q2Kw [78]), and traditional agent-based (LLM-D [30]). Evaluations use LLM-based and human metrics.

IV-B1 LLM Evaluation Results

Table I shows that NAMeGEn consistently outperforms all baselines across backbones and metrics, confirming its effectiveness in NCB. Fig. 3 further shows it achieves the lowest EC_std, IC_std, and CC_std, highlighting its superior balance in EUOs, IIOs, and their combination. We next analyze the HMOO challenge from three perspectives: overall, EUOs, and IIOs.

Overall, Table I shows that backbone differences impact performance partially. Firstly, Chinese-oriented models generally outperform English ones. For instance, under the Base, CC reaches 80.66 with Qwen but drops to 75.11 with Mistral. Similarly, models with stronger contextual understanding (e.g., DeepSeek, GPT-4o) perform better. In Few-shot, for example, CC with GPT-4o reaches 86.51, which is 5.94 points higher than with Mistral (80.57). In contrast to other methods’ fluctuation across backbones, NAMeGEn shows consistently strong performance, demonstrating superior robustness and cross-backbone generalizability. Otherwise, Fig. 3 shows that balance mainly depends on methods, not backbones. Although all methods boost diversity (DIV rise compared to Base in Table I), NAMeGEn achieves the highest creative diversity, likely owing to more effective iterative guidance.

For multi-EUOs’ optimization in the NCB task, in-context methods demonstrate better improvements in both creativity and balance compared to reasoning-based ones. As shown in Table I, reasoning-based methods provide limited achievement in explicit objectives, with notable declines in some cases. For example, with GLM-4, CoT’s EC is 80.25, which is lower than the Base’s 88.37 (a drop of 8.12), highlighting CoT’s limitations in CNLG, as also discussed in [87]. In contrast, few-shot improves explicit performance by introducing additional examples (e.g., Few-shot’s EC rises from Base’s 88.37 to 94.10 on GLM-4). Regarding balance, Fig. 3 shows that few-shot still significantly outperforms reasoning-based methods (CoT, TDB). The underlying cause is shown in Fig. 4a: reasoning-based methods perform well on common objectives (e.g., O1, O5) but struggle with others. Notably, most baselines also underperform on complex, rarer objectives (e.g., O3, O4). This imbalance highlights the limited their limited adaptability to diverse creative objectives. Retrieval-based methods offer cultural knowledge that helps on objectives like O1 but introduce noise that negatively impacts others (O2–O5). Consequently, Q2Kw often performs worse than Base in terms of EC and EC_std (see Table I, Fig. 3). Traditional agent-based methods such as LLM-D struggle on O4 (Fig. 4a), indicating a need for more effective information expansion beyond user input. Accordingly, NAMeGEn integrates the strengths of in-context learning with more accurate expansion and retrieval to reduce noise. Supported by explicit objective guidance and iterative dynamic optimization, NAMeGEn demonstrates strong adaptability to diverse EUOs. It achieves the highest EC and lowest EC_std (Table I, Fig. 3), validating NAMeGEn’s effectiveness in optimizing multi-EUOs for NCB.

As shown in Table I, all baselines achieve an unsatisfactory for explainability (IC<<90). Fig. 4b offers a fine-grained view. Firstly, in reasoning-based methods, CoT exhibits unstable and poor ACC, CRC, and LR across backbones, with no clear trend. Although TDB improves logic (↑LR), ACC and CRC remain unstable, explaining their underperformance for IIOs’ optimization (e.g., higher IC_std for CoT in Fig.3). Few-shot enhances explanation completeness (↑CRC) but increases hallucinations (↓ACC) due to noisy examples, harming both overall interpretability (e.g., IC drops from 79.29 to 77.68 on GPT-4o, Table I). Similarly, retrieval-based methods help mitigate hallucinations (↑ACC) at the cost of completeness (↓CRC), yet the ACC gain yields better interpretability scores overall (e.g., IC from Base’s 76.29 to 80.05 on Qwen). Traditional agent-based methods (e.g., LLM-D) improve logic and accuracy (↑LR, ↑ACC) of explanation but show inconsistent completeness (CRC), resulting in partial interpretability gains without fully optimizing IIOs. In summary, baselines fail to balance and optimize all implicit objectives fully. In contrast, NAMeGEn’s multi-agent collaborative optimization achieves superior interpretability. As Fig. 5 shows, NAMeGEn’s results cluster near the Pareto front with high scores (80+), demonstrating effective multi-objective coordination. Overall, NAMeGEn robustly optimizes EUOs, IIOs, and their combination, validating its effectiveness on HMOO.

IV-B2 Human Evaluation and Correlation

We compare three improved baselines (TDB, Few-shot, LLM-D). Fig.6a shows a Pearson correlation of r=0.68(>0.5),p=0.0003(<0.001)r=0.68(>0.5),p=0.0003(<0.001), indicating a statistically significant positive correlation between human and LLM evaluations. In Fig.6b, annotators preferred NAMeGEn in 81% of cases, far surpassing Few-shot (13%), LLM-D (3%), and TDB (3%). These results align with LLM-based evaluations, validating both NAMeGEn’s superiority and the reliability of automatic metrics.

IV-C Ablation Study

We conduct ablation studies on the following settings: wo/ Imp&Exp: Excludes both descriptions IdescI_{\text{desc}} and requirements IreqsI_{\text{reqs}}, as well as the implicit and explicit evaluations dependent on them. wo/ Imp: Excludes IreqsI_{\text{reqs}} and implicit evaluation process based on them. wo/ Exp: Excludes IdescI_{\text{desc}} and explicit evaluation process based on them. wo/ evalGen: Removes all evaluation processes involving both IdescI_{\text{desc}} and IreqsI_{\text{reqs}} as criteria (i.e., implicit and explicit evaluation during generation). wo/ R: Removes the retrieval. wo/ evalR: Excludes evaluation of the retrieved content.

The results of the ablation study are summarized in Table II. In wo/ Imp&Exp, most metrics exhibit a notable performance drop, highlighting the importance of detailed objective guidance and evaluation feedback in HMOO. Moreover, the sharp decline in ACC (from 94.55 to 63.25) in the absence of Imp&Exp highlights NAMeGEn’s effectiveness in mitigating hallucination. Compared to NAMeGEn, the higher LR suggests that the additional information may introduce noise, which in turn slightly compromises logical rationality. A finer-grained ablation shows that wo/ Imp has a greater effect on implicit objective completion (IC from 92.7 to 89.54), while wo/ Exp more significantly impacts explicit objective balance (EC_std from 5.95 to 7.57), confirming the effectiveness of our approach in both aspects. In the EC metric, wo/ Imp performs worse than wo/ Exp. This indicates that optimizing IIOs helps reach EUOs potentially, which leads to greater improvements in EC. Furthermore, given the potential correlation between EUOs and IIOs, such as there is no separation between clearer explanations and explicit objective completion. Therefore, both implicit and explicit information and evaluation influence the completeness and balance of both types of objectives. Finally, the decline in all metrics for wo/ evalGen demonstrates the effectiveness of our method’s dynamic evaluation strategy. Compared to wo/ Imp and wo/ Exp, wo/ evalGen shows a greater decrease in ACC, indicating that the evaluation stage has a better effect on hallucination mitigation. The results in Table III show that wo/ evalR has a decline in EC(c), indicating that evaluating retrieval content helps find the matcher knowledge for user needs. The wo/ R performs poorly in ACC(p), revealing that the retrieval helps mitigate the LLMs’ hallucination of domain knowledge. In summary, the ablation results validate the effectiveness of different components of our multi-agent collaborative framework with dynamic iterative HMOO.

IV-D Efficiency Analysis

Fig. 7 shows the interaction requests and density distribution at different stages of NAMeGEn. Fig. 7a exhibits the distribution of total API requests during the task. Most require only 5-10 requests, with a peak around 6, indicating high interaction efficiency, and can converge. Fig. 7b shows the distribution of interaction rounds across different stages. In the retrieval stage, most interactions are concentrated in lower rounds, indicating quick information retrieval. In the generation and evaluation stages, most require only 2-3 rounds of generation and 1-2 rounds of evaluation, reflecting optimization efficiency. Overall, these distribution features exhibit a clear concentration with a sparse tail, where the proportion of low-frequency, high-round requests is lower. This indicates that NAMeGEn can achieve task completion with limited interaction costs in most cases, demonstrating excellent convergence and stability. Fig. 8 illustrates the dynamics score during NAMeGEn’s iterative process. The threshold (dashed line) is initially set at a higher level and gradually decreases over iterations, allowing for adaptive convergence control. The actual scores (solid lines) generally stay above these thresholds, suggesting that the method consistently meets or exceeds evaluation criteria. This indicates a strong convergence capability of our method.

IV-E Qualitative Evaluation

Since DeepSeek performs the best among Chinese LLMs, we choose it as the backbone for qualitative evaluation. As shown in Fig. 9a, NAMeGEn outperforms Few-shot. We also test other tasks (slogan design), with results shown in Fig. 9b. Without EUOs, our method can also automatically resolve some EUOs ( Brand positioning, Target Audience, Creative Expression). The base method is inputting the query and EUOs into DeepSeek without any extra methods. Compared to Base, our results are more aligned with user needs. These comparisons in Fig. 9 show NAMeGEn’s effectiveness in real-world applications.

V Conclusion

This paper presents the NAMeGEn framework, a novel multi-agent collaborative approach designed to address the challenges of Hybrid Multi-Objective Optimization (HMOO) in Creative Natural Language Generation (CNLG), particularly in short-text tasks like Naming Chinese Babies (NCB). By employing a dynamic iterative hybrid multi-objective optimization strategy, NAMeGEn meets user-specified objectives while ensuring high-quality explanations in terms of factuality, completeness, and clarity. Experimental results on the CBNames benchmark demonstrate the framework’s flexibility and adaptability, consistently achieving excellent optimization results across various backbone models. Furthermore, NAMeGEn outperforms existing methods by reducing hallucination issues and providing more logically coherent and completely generated names. This work contributes to advancing the field of CNLG and lays a foundation for future research in the domain of multi-objective optimization.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
